program: Inglês Geral & Intercultural -- Fluência e Autonomia
hub_subtitle: Inglês para a vida real — falar, entender qualquer sotaque e ter autonomia no idioma

lesson.menu_desc: Shoes at the door in Norway, an aunt in India who says you must eat more and an English landlady who says you might want to. Tonight, have to, mustn’t, should and had better -- and how advice sounds in each culture
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- What Should I Do?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 17 -- What Should I Do?

listenings.text: My name is Ingrid, and I live in Bergen, on the west coast of Norway. People always ask me about the rules of a Norwegian home, so here they are. First, you have to take your shoes off at the door. Nobody will tell you, but everybody will look at your feet. Second, you don't have to bring a big present. A small thing is perfect, and something too expensive can make people uncomfortable. Third, if dinner is at six, you should arrive at six. Not at ten past six, and please, not at a quarter to. And one more thing. When a Norwegian gives you advice, it sounds very soft. We say, maybe you could, or it might be an idea to. My Brazilian friend Camila did not understand that at first. I told her, it might be an idea to bring a warmer coat. She thought it was a small suggestion. It was minus twelve that week. She learned.

Hello, I am Arjun, from Pune, in India. In my family, advice is very direct. My aunt says, you must eat more, you are too thin. You should call your mother every day. You have to come for lunch on Sunday. For a foreigner, this sounds like orders. For us, it is love. If my aunt does not tell me what to do, I think she is angry with me. Then I went to study in Manchester, in England, and everything was upside down. In my first week, my landlady said, you might want to put the bins out on Thursday night. I thought, okay, it is optional. I did not do it. On Friday she knocked on my door, very politely, and said, the bins really must go out on Thursday. So in India, must can be love. In England, might want to can be a rule. Now, when an English person gives me soft advice, I always follow it.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: A small social mistake that makes you feel embarrassed
Not required, so you can choose
Trying to help, even if the result is not perfect
To think that something is not acceptable
The rules of polite behavior in a place or a group
Rules that everybody follows but nobody writes down
Required by a rule, so you have no choice
To be supposed to do something because it is normal

vocab.text: Three of tonight’s words are whole expressions: a rule of thumb, when in Rome and to take something the wrong way. Notice the pair mandatory and optional: they are the formal cousins of tonight’s grammar — you have to and you don’t have to.

items.situation: A friend from abroad is staying at your house for the first time. Tell her one rule of the house.
tips: You have to close the front gate. You don’t have to take your shoes off.
Have to for a rule, don’t have to for a choice.

items.situation: A friend is going to Norway in January. Give her strong advice, with a warning.
tips: You’d better bring warm boots, or your feet will freeze.
Had better = advice + a warning. No to after it.

items.situation: Explain the difference: you mustn’t smoke here / you don’t have to smoke here.
tips: Mustn’t = it is forbidden. Don’t have to = you can choose. Very different!
This is the biggest trap of the lesson.

items.situation: Tell me something you had to do last week. Careful with the past.
tips: Last week I had to take my car to the mechanic.
Must has no past. Use had to.

items.situation: A British friend says: you might want to bring an umbrella. What does she really mean?
tips: She means: bring an umbrella! Soft advice can be a strong suggestion.

items.situation: Give a foreign visitor one piece of advice about Brazil.
tips: You should try the cheese bread, and you’d better not drive in Sao Paulo at six.
This one has no grammar target. Say the true thing.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: have to + verb = necessary, often a rule from outside: You have to take your shoes off.
must + verb = necessary, the speaker feels it: I must call my mother tonight.
don’t have to = not necessary, you choose: You don’t have to bring a gift.
mustn’t = forbidden: You mustn’t smoke inside. It is NOT the same as don’t have to.
should / ought to = advice: You should try the brown cheese.
had better = strong advice + a warning: You’d better bring warm socks.
No to after must, should and had better. The past of must is had to.
And the one that is not grammar: a direct you must can be love, and a soft you might want to can be a rule. Listen to who is speaking.

lesson.grammar_point: modals of obligation and advice: have to, must, should and had better
